title: HARRISON v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
summary: In Harrison v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Jean Harrison, a Romany Traveller, brought a case against the United Kingdom after being refused planning permission to live in her caravan on her own land in Christchurch, Dorset. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities, who often face significant barriers to securing lawful accommodation that respects their traditional way of life. Ms. Harrison, together with her elderly mother and grandchildren, had lived in caravans on the site since 1985, in an area known for its longstanding Traveller presence. Despite this, local authorities denied her planning permission, citing Green Belt policies and concerns about the visual impact on the rural landscape. Enforcement notices required her to remove her caravan, and appeals to planning authorities and the Secretary of State were unsuccessful, even though alternative sites offered were unsuitable for her family’s needs. Ms. Harrison argued that these measures interfered with her right to respect for her home and family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and amounted to discrimination under Article 14. The European Court of Human Rights, however, declared the application inadmissible, finding that the national authorities had sufficiently considered her interests and that the planning controls pursued legitimate aims. This case reflects the ongoing struggle of Roma and Traveller communities in Europe to secure adequate accommodation and recognition of their cultural needs, against a backdrop of restrictive planning policies and historical marginalisation.
